The integral is finite because a continuous function on a compact closed interval is bounded. Nonnegativity is immediate, and absolute homogeneity of a norm follows from ∣cf(x)∣=∣c∣∣f(x)∣. The pointwise triangle inequality gives
∥f+g∥≤∫−11​(∣f(x)∣+∣g(x)∣)dx=∥f∥+∥g∥.
(1)
For positive definiteness, if f(x0​)=0, continuity gives a relative interval of positive length on which ∣f(x)∣≥∣f(x0​)∣/2. Its integral is positive, including when x0​ is an endpoint. Thus ∥f∥=0 implies f=0, and this is a norm on the given vector space.
For the given sequence,
∥fn​∥=2∫01​xndx=n+12​,∥fn​−fm​∥≤n+12​+m+12​.
(2)
The last bound tends to zero as both indices tend to infinity, proving the Cauchy sequence property. Moreover, the sequence converges to the zero function in this norm:
∥fn​−0∥=n+12​⟶0.​
(3)
There is no conflict with the nonzero endpoint values: convergence in this norm does not imply pointwise convergence.

Write the cone as z=rcotα, with r the distance from its axis and 0<α<π/2. Its Euclidean metric gives
ds2=dr2+r2dθ2+dz2=csc2αdr2+r2dθ2.
(4)
Consequently a differentiable path expressed as r=r(θ) has arc length
S=∫r2+csc2α(r′)2​dθ.​
(5)
For L(r,r′)=r2+csc2α(r′)2​, the Euler-Lagrange equation has the Beltrami identity because L has no explicit θ dependence:
L−r′∂r′∂L​=Lr2​=C.
(6)
For a nonradial minimizing path, C>0. Rearranging and integrating gives
(r′)2=sin2αr2(C2r2​−1),rcos((θ−θ0​)sinα)=C.​
(7)
The endpoint conditions determine C and θ0​ on the selected angular branch.
To verify that this stationary path really minimizes arc length, use the local isometry from a circular cone to the plane. Set s=r/sinα and ϕ=θsinα; then ds2+s2dϕ2 is the plane metric. The displayed path is a straight line scos(ϕ−ϕ0​)=C/sinα, so its segment realizes the plane distance. Choose endpoint angular lifts with ∣Δθ∣≤π; then ∣Δϕ∣<π, and the joining segment avoids the apex. Its length is
sinα1​r12​+r22​−2r1​r2​cos(sinαΔθ)​.
(8)
Other lifts with developed angular difference less than π give at least this distance; an angular change of at least π has infimum at least s1​+s2​, attained only if passage through the apex is allowed. This proves the global choice above. Endpoints on a common generator have the radial segment as shortest path, which is the limiting case omitted by the r(θ) parametrization. If an endpoint is the apex, its shortest path is a generator. Thus shortest paths are straight segments after developing the cone.

4F OurBigBook.com
Let T be the isometry. Since T(0)=0, it preserves norms, and the polarization identity applied to distances gives ⟨T(x),T(y)⟩=⟨x,y⟩. For an orthonormal basis e1​,e2​,e3​, the vectors T(ei​) are again an orthonormal basis, and
⟨T(x),T(ei​)⟩=⟨x,ei​⟩.
(12)
Expanding in that basis proves T(x)=∑i​⟨x,ei​⟩T(ei​). Hence T is a linear map represented by an orthogonal matrix Q.
A reflection in a hyperplane with nonzero normal v is Hv​(x)=x−2⟨x,v⟩v/⟨v,v⟩. If Qe1​=e1​, choose v=Qe1​−e1​. Because ∥Qe1​∥=∥e1​∥, substitution shows Hv​Qe1​=e1​. If they agree, no reflection is needed. The resulting orthogonal transformation fixes e1​ and preserves its orthogonal complement. Apply the same construction there to fix e2​; the second normal is perpendicular to e1​, so the first vector remains fixed. Finally the restriction to the remaining line is either the identity or negation; in the latter case a third reflection, normal to e3​, fixes it. Reversing these steps writes Q as a product of at most three reflections, each in a plane through the origin. This proves the three-dimensional case of the Cartan–Dieudonné theorem.
Three reflections are sometimes necessary. The map −I is the product of the three coordinate-plane reflections. Its determinant is −1, excluding zero or two reflections. A single plane reflection fixes a two-dimensional vector subspace, whereas −I fixes only zero, excluding one. Thus the bound is sharp.

Player A maximizes the payoff, while B minimizes it. The fourth row is strictly worse for A than the first in every column, so remove A4​ by dominated strategy elimination. On the remaining rows, column B3​ is strictly better for B than B2​, so remove B2​. Now A3​ is strictly worse than A2​ in the two remaining columns. The reduced zero-sum game has payoff matrix
(4−2​−53​),
(13)
with rows A1​,A2​ and columns B1​,B3​.
If A uses mixed strategy (p,1−p), the expected payoffs against these columns are −2+6p and 3−8p. The first increases and the second decreases, so their minimum is maximized where they are equal: 14p=5. Thus
A: (5/14,9/14,0,0),v=1/7.​
(14)
For an optimality certificate, B uses mixed strategy (q,0,1−q), making A's first two row payoffs −5+9q and 3−5q. Equality gives q=4/7. Against this B strategy the four row payoffs are (1/7,1/7,−6/7,−6/7), while against the displayed A strategy the three column payoffs are (1/7,13/7,1/7). Therefore A guarantees 1/7 and B holds A to 1/7, verifying the value of a zero-sum game and the original, unreduced mixed strategy.

(α−λI)βx=β(α−λI)x=0.

Thus each eigenspace of α is an invariant subspace for β.
If α=β2, the two endomorphisms commute. The n distinct real eigenvalues of α have one-dimensional real eigenspaces, since their direct sum is the n-dimensional vector space. 8C OurBigBook.com
With polar unit vectors er​=(cosθ,sinθ,0) and eθ​=(−sinθ,cosθ,0), the second term is Γeθ​/(2πr). It is tangent to circles, independent of z, and has zero divergence and zero vorticity away from the axis. Its singular axis carries a line vortex; adding the constant velocity field gives a uniform flow plus that line vortex.
The counterclockwise circulation around a positively oriented loop is ∮u⋅dr. For a radius-R circle, the uniform flow contributes zero and the line vortex contributes
∮CR​​2πRΓ​eθ​⋅Reθ​dθ=Γ.
(20)
Any loop winding once around the axis has the same circulation, by Stokes theorem in the nonsingular intervening region.
On CR​, n=er​, u⋅n=Ucosθ, and dl=Rdθ. Thus
∮CR​​(u⋅n)udl=RU2ex​∫02π​cosθdθ+2πUΓ​∫02π​cosθeθ​dθ=21​Γ×U​.
(21)
In fact this equality holds for every R>0 for the stated field, since the remaining vector integral is (0,π,0).
This is the advective part of the momentum flux. To obtain the force, include pressure. For steady irrotational flow, the Bernoulli equation gives
p=p∞​−2ρ​(∣u∣2−U2)=p∞​+2πRρUΓsinθ​−8π2R2ρΓ2​.
(22)
The constant terms integrate to zero against n; the remaining pressure contribution is ∮pndl=ρΓ×U/2. The total outward momentum flux plus pressure term is therefore ρΓ×U, the force of the obstacle on the fluid. The opposite force, of fluid on the obstacle per unit span, is
F=ρU×Γ.​
(23)
This is the Kutta–Joukowski theorem, with positive Γ defined counterclockwise: positive U and Γ give force in the negative y direction. For an actual two-dimensional aerofoil, faster-decaying far-field terms do not change this limit. The displayed advective integral supplies half the lift; pressure supplies the other half.

9G OurBigBook.com
The discriminant of a binary quadratic form is d=b2−4ac; it is unchanged by a unimodular matrix change of integral variables and satisfies d≡0 or 1(mod4). For such a d, the discriminant criterion for prime representation by a binary quadratic form says that some integral binary quadratic form of discriminant of a binary quadratic form d represents an odd prime p exactly when d is a square modulo p, including zero. Equivalently,
there is an integer B with B2≡d(mod4p).​
(24)
These versions agree: a square root modulo p can be chosen even when d≡0(mod4) and odd when d≡1(mod4), by adding p if needed, and then the Chinese remainder theorem applies.
For completeness, if f(x,y)=p, then (x,y) is primitive, since any common divisor would have its square divide p. Complete (x,y) to a basis of Z2 with determinant one using Bézout's identity. The transformed binary quadratic form has leading coefficient p and discriminant of a binary quadratic form B2−4pC=d. Conversely, a suitable B makes [p,B,(B2−d)/(4p)] an integral binary quadratic form representing p at (1,0).
For x2+3y2, the discriminant of a binary quadratic form is −12. The prime 3 is represented. If p=3 is represented, reducing modulo 3 gives p≡x2≡1(mod3), which also excludes p=2. To prove sufficiency for p≡1(mod3), quadratic reciprocity gives
(p−3​)=(p−1​)(p3​)=(3p​)=1.
(25)
The criterion constructs a positive definite binary quadratic form [p,B,C] of discriminant of a binary quadratic form −12. It is primitive: a common divisor of its coefficients would divide p, and if that divisor were p, then p2 would divide 12, impossible for p=2,3.
We must still establish that this form is equivalent to x2+3y2, rather than merely some form of the same discriminant of a binary quadratic form. In a positive definite integral binary quadratic form, replace x by x+ky to arrange ∣b∣≤a. If c<a, apply (x,y)↦(−y,x) and repeat. Each such exchange strictly decreases the positive integer leading coefficient, so this reduction algorithm for a positive definite binary quadratic form terminates with ∣b∣≤a≤c. Then 12=4ac−b2≥3a2, so a≤2. With a=1, parity forces b=0, giving c=3. With a=2, the only integral choices are b=±2,c=2, and these are not primitive. Thus every primitive positive definite binary quadratic form of discriminant of a binary quadratic form −12 is equivalent to [1,0,3], and preserves its represented integers. Therefore
p=x2+3y2 for integers x,y⟺p=3 or p≡1(mod3).​
(26)

A photon of wavelength λ has energy E=hν=hc/λ and momentum p=(h/λ)n^ along its propagation direction.
The specified Compton scattering formula requires the electron to be initially at rest in the frame where the wavelengths and angle are measured. This initial-rest assumption is implicit in the printed request; it is not valid for arbitrary initial electron momentum. Use four-momentum with Minkowski metric signature (+−−−): initially P=(mc,0), while K=(E/c,(E/c)n^) and K′=(E′/c,(E′/c)n^′) are null. Conservation gives P′=P+K−K′, and the outgoing electron satisfies the same mass-shell condition P′2=P2=m2c2. Hence
P⋅(K−K′)=K⋅K′,m(E−E′)=c2EE′​(1−cosθ).
(27)
After dividing by EE′ and substituting the photon energy relation,
E′1​−E1​=mc21−cosθ​,λ′−λ=mch​(1−cosθ).​
(28)
The scale h/(mc) is the electron Compton wavelength. For a moving initial electron, the earlier invariant identity remains valid, but P⋅K includes its initial velocity and the wavelength shift is different.

11F OurBigBook.com
The contraction mapping theorem states that a contraction mapping f of a nonempty complete metric space into itself has a unique fixed point. More explicitly, if d(f(x),f(y))≤qd(x,y) with 0≤q<1, iteration from any x0​ converges to that fixed point.
To prove this, put xn+1​=f(xn​). Induction gives d(xn+1​,xn​)≤qnd(x1​,x0​), so for m>n the triangle inequality gives
d(xm​,xn​)≤∑j=nm−1​qjd(x1​,x0​)≤1−qqn​d(x1​,x0​).
(29)
Thus (xn​) is a Cauchy sequence, and completeness supplies a limit x∗​. A contraction mapping is continuous, so f(x∗​)=limf(xn​)=limxn+1​=x∗​. Two fixed points satisfy d(x∗​,y∗​)≤qd(x∗​,y∗​), forcing equality of the points. Passing to the limit in the bound also gives the useful error estimate d(xn​,x∗​)≤qnd(x1​,x0​)/(1−q).
For the function space, take X nonempty; otherwise the supremum in the printed definition is undefined without a convention. Boundedness of X makes the uniform metric ρ(f,g) finite. Nonnegativity and symmetry follow from d; ρ(f,g)=0 means f(x)=g(x) at every x. Taking suprema in d(f(x),h(x))≤d(f(x),g(x))+d(g(x),h(x)) proves the triangle inequality. Hence ρ is a metric.
Suppose (fn​) is a Cauchy sequence for this uniform metric. At each x, d(fn​(x),fm​(x))≤ρ(fn​,fm​), so completeness of X supplies a value f(x)=limn​fn​(x). Given ε>0, choose N with ρ(fn​,fm​)<ε/2 for all n,m≥N. Fix n≥N and let m→∞ pointwise; then d(fn​(x),f(x))≤ε/2 for every x. Thus ρ(fn​,f)≤ε/2<ε. The uniform limit theorem makes this limit continuous, so f∈F. This proves the completeness of the continuous-map space in the uniform metric.
Finally fix f∈C with contraction constant qf​<1, and write xf​=θ(f) and xg​=θ(g). Using the fixed point equations,
d(xg​,xf​)≤d(g(xg​),f(xg​))+d(f(xg​),f(xf​))≤ρ(f,g)+qf​d(xg​,xf​).
(30)
Therefore the fixed-point stability in the uniform metric estimate is
d(θ(g),θ(f))≤1−qf​ρ(f,g)​.​
(31)
Choosing ρ(f,g)<(1−qf​)ε proves continuity of θ at every f. The estimate uses the constant of the fixed map f only; it does not require a common contraction constant for all nearby g.

Assume the impulse point is in the interior, 0<a<l. Expand the displacement in the fixed-end Fourier sine series
y(x,t)=∑n=1∞​Tn​(t)sinlnπx​,αn​=lnπc​.
(32)
Orthogonality gives the initial velocity coefficient by applying the Dirac delta to the sine function:
Tn​(0)=0,Tn′​(0)=l2​∫0l​δ(x−a)sinlnπx​dx=l2​sinlnπa​.
(33)
Substitution in the wave equation yields Tn′′​+2kTn′​+αn2​Tn​=0. For k<αn​, its roots are −k±iωn​, where ωn​=αn2​−k2​. The two initial conditions determine
Tn​(t)=l2​sinlnπa​e−ktωn​sin(ωn​t)​.
(34)
Hence the normalized velocity-impulse Green function for a damped string is
y(x,t)=l2​n=1∑∞​sinlnπa​sinlnπx​e−ktαn2​−k2​sin(αn2​−k2​t)​.​
(35)
For a mode with critical damping, use the limit e−ktt in place of the time factor. For k>αn​, put ηn​=k2−αn2​​ and use e−ktsinh(ηn​t)/ηn​. These choices solve the same modal ordinary differential equation and initial conditions, so the formula covers arbitrary k>0. The impulse initial velocity is a distribution, so initial differentiation of the series is interpreted distributionally.
The printed formula requires correction: the factor depending on n must lie inside the sum, and sine-mode normalization requires 2/l, rather than 2. The printed slash after the final sine is also stray. Direct differentiation at t=0 verifies the corrected normalization: the initial sine coefficients are exactly those of δ(x−a).

A mode has dimensionless damping ratio k/αn​, and characteristic roots
s±​=−k±k2−αn2​​.
(36)
If k/αn​≪1, the normal mode oscillates at ωn​=αn​+O(k2/αn​) with exponentially decaying envelope e−kt. As k→0, the solution approaches the undamped wave equation response.
If k/αn​≫1, the roots are real and negative, with
s+​=−2kαn2​​+O(αn4​/k3),s−​=−2k+2kαn2​​+O(αn4​/k3).
(37)
The mode has a fast transient and a slow nonoscillatory relaxation. After the fast transient, neglecting ytt​ gives the diffusion equation yt​≃c2yxx​/(2k) for these long-wavelength modes. At k=αn​, the repeated root produces te−kt: this is critical damping.
Thus the critical parameter is k/αn​=1 for each mode, and the fundamental threshold is
πckl​=1.​
(38)
When k<πc/l every mode is oscillatory. For any fixed, finite k, sufficiently large n still gives oscillatory modes, so large damping of the lowest modes does not mean that every mode of the full string is overdamped.

Put h=f−g. Choose a disc about z0​ contained in the domain D. Part (a) gives a convergent Taylor series there, and the accumulating zeros together with part (b) force all its coefficients to vanish. Thus h=0 near z0​.
To propagate this to the entire domain, define
S={z∈D:h(n)(z)=0 for every n≥0}.
(42)
The set is nonempty by the preceding local argument. Each derivative is continuous, so S is closed relative to D as the intersection of their zero sets. If z∈S, its Taylor series is zero on a disc about z, and all derivatives vanish throughout that disc; hence S is open relative to D. Connectedness forces S=D. Therefore f=g throughout D, proving the identity theorem for holomorphic functions rather than merely invoking it.

Let f have the stated zeros but not be identically zero. The origin is an isolated singularity. If it were a removable singularity, the extended holomorphic function would have zeros accumulating at an interior point. The proof in part (c) would force the extension, and then f on its domain, to be identically zero.
If the origin were a pole of order m, then g(z)=zmf(z) would have a holomorphic extension with g(0)=0. Continuity would make g nonzero on a small disc, so f would have no zeros in its punctured disc, again a contradiction. The classification of isolated singularities leaves only an essential singularity at the origin. This argument applies to every function in part (d), not just the particular sine example.

Work first on the unit sphere. A spherical lune of angle α has area 2α: its fraction of sphere area is α/(2π). The three great circles extending the sides of a nondegenerate spherical triangle divide the sphere into four antipodal pairs of triangular regions. Call the desired region T, of area A, and its three adjacent regions T1​,T2​,T3​, of areas A1​,A2​,A3​. These four regions contain one region from each antipodal pair, so A+A1​+A2​+A3​=2π. The lune at each vertex consists of T and one of these adjacent regions. Therefore, if the three interior angles are α,β,γ,
2(α+β+γ)=3A+A1​+A2​+A3​=2A+2π,
(44)
which proves the spherical excess formula, the spherical-triangle form of the Gauss-Bonnet theorem:
A=α+β+γ−π.​
(45)
For a sphere of radius s, multiply this area by s2.
Triangulate a convex spherical n-gon by diagonals from a vertex. There are n−2 spherical triangles, and their angles add to the polygon's interior angle sum. Thus its unit-sphere area is
A=i=1∑n​αi​−(n−2)π.​
(46)
For a nondegenerate convex regular polygon in an open hemisphere, area is positive and each angle is less than π, giving (n−2)π/n<α<π. Every angle in this interval occurs. Indeed place n vertices at equal longitude spacings and colatitude t∈(0,π/2) about a pole, and join consecutive vertices by shorter great circle arcs. The polygon is convex and regular. Split a central isosceles spherical triangle along the perpendicular to its edge. The resulting right spherical triangle has angles π/n, α/2, π/2, and hypotenuse t. The angular spherical law of cosines yields
0=−cos(π/n)cos(α/2)+sin(π/n)sin(α/2)cost,
(47)
so cot(α/2)=costtan(π/n). As t increases from 0 to π/2, α increases continuously through exactly
nn−2​π<α<π,n≥3.​
(48)
The endpoints are degenerate limits, not strict convex polygons.
For the spherical triangle reflection group, positive area requires 1/p+1/q+1/r>1. Each angle is less than π, so the integer denominators are at least two. Arrange p≤q≤r. If p≥3 the sum is at most one, hence p=2. If q≥4 the sum is again at most one; thus either q=2 and any r≥2 works, or q=3 and r=3,4,5. These triangles exist, for example as the reflection chambers of a regular dihedral configuration, tetrahedron, cube, and dodecahedron, respectively.
To count group elements using the assumed tessellation, first label the original triangle's three vertices by their types and propagate these labels through side reflections. Around a type-p vertex there are 2p sectors; the associated alternating reflections make a full turn and return the labels unchanged. The same holds at the other types. Every closed path in the dual tessellation is generated by these circuits around vertices, since the sphere is simply connected. Thus the labels are globally consistent, including when two angle denominators coincide. Every generated isometry preserves these labels. An element stabilizing a triangle therefore fixes its three vertices and is the identity. Consequently group elements correspond bijectively to triangles, and area gives
∣G∣=π(1/p+1/q+1/r−1)4π​.
(49)
The possibilities, including permutations of the entries, are
(p,q,r)(2,2,n), n≥2(2,3,3)(2,3,4)(2,3,5)​∣G∣4n2448120​​​.
(50)
Here is an explicit dodecahedron construction for the last case, avoiding an assumption about which vertices of the tessellation to join. Put φ=(1+5​)/2, and take the convex hull of the twenty points
(±1,±1,±1),(0,±φ−1,±φ),(±φ−1,±φ,0),(±φ,0,±φ−1),
(51)
with independent signs. They all have squared radius three. The supporting plane φy+z=φ2 contains the five vertices
(1,1,1), (φ−1,φ,0), (−φ−1,φ,0), (−1,1,1), (0,φ−1,φ)
(52)
in cyclic order. Consecutive distances are 2/φ, and nonconsecutive distances are 2, so this is a regular pentagon. Changing the two signs in its normal (0,φ,1) and cyclically permuting coordinates gives twelve supporting planes, all with a congruent pentagon. Each listed vertex lies on three of these faces; the sixty face-edge incidences pair into thirty edges. The faces form a closed convex polyhedral surface with 20−30+12=2, hence exhaust the boundary of the convex hull. This constructs a regular dodecahedron.
Choose the spherical directions of a face center F=(0,φ,1), the midpoint M=(0,φ,0) of its edge between (±φ−1,φ,0), and that edge's endpoint V=(φ−1,φ,0). Normalize these to the unit sphere. The three side planes of triangle FMV are x=0, z=0, and n⋅x=0 with n=(−φ,φ−1,−1). Their reflections are coordinate sign changes in the first two cases and
H(x)=x−21​(n⋅x)n
(53)
in the third, since ∥n∥2=4. Substitution in the twenty listed vertices, using φ2=φ+1, shows that all three reflections permute the vertex set. The side-plane angles give interior angles π/2 at M, π/3 at V, and π/5 at F because ∣nz​∣/∥n∥=1/2 and ∣nx​∣/∥n∥=φ/2=cos(π/5). Thus this triangle is congruent to Δ, and its side-generated group is G, conjugated by the aligning isometry.
It already has 120 elements. Conversely, a symmetry of the dodecahedron is determined by the image of one face, one vertex on that face, and the orientation along its boundary: there are at most 12⋅5⋅2=120 choices. An isometry fixing these choices fixes that face pointwise and must preserve the polyhedron's interior side, hence is the identity. Therefore the complete symmetry group of the constructed dodecahedron is G, including orientation-reversing symmetries.

A balanced transportation problem chooses nonnegative shipments xij​ minimizing ∑ij​cij​xij​, subject to ∑j​xij​=si​ and ∑i​xij​=dj​, where the total supply equals total demand. For multipliers ui​,vj​, its Lagrangian is
L=∑ij​cij​xij​+∑i​ui​(si​−∑j​xij​)+∑j​vj​(dj​−∑i​xij​)=∑i​ui​si​+∑j​vj​dj​+∑ij​(cij​−ui​−vj​)xij​.
(54)
Taking its infimum over xij​≥0 produces the linear programming duality problem of maximizing ∑i​ui​si​+∑j​vj​dj​ subject to ui​+vj​≤cij​. These are the transportation dual potentials.
The transportation simplex algorithm starts with a feasible transportation spanning tree of m+n−1 basic entries, obtainable by filling the north-west available cell with the smaller remaining supply or demand. Set ui​+vj​=cij​ on basic cells; this determines all potentials up to adding a constant to all ui​ and subtracting it from all vj​. If all nonbasic reduced costs rij​=cij​−ui​−vj​ are nonnegative, feasibility and the dual bound prove optimality. Otherwise let a negative-cost cell enter. It closes a unique cycle in the basic tree. Alternate additions and subtractions around that cycle and choose the largest amount preserving nonnegativity, namely the minimum shipment on the subtraction cells. A cell that reaches zero leaves the basis. The cost changes by the entering reduced cost times the pivot amount. Zero basic cells and an anti-cycling rule can handle degeneracy; all pivots below are nondegenerate.
The north-west initial shipment matrix is
X0​=​1400​22460​03840​​,C0​=1156.
(55)
With u1​=0, its transportation dual potentials are u=(0,1,0) and v=(5,9,5). The most negative reduced cost is r32​=−7. The cycle is +(3,2),−(3,3),+(2,3),−(2,2); the pivot amount is min(40,46)=40. Hence
X1​=​1400​22640​0780​​,C1​=1156−7⋅40=876.
(56)
Now u=(0,1,−7) and v=(5,9,5). Enter (1,3), of reduced cost −4, on cycle +(1,3),−(1,2),+(2,2),−(2,3). The amount is min(22,78)=22, giving
X2​=​1400​02840​22560​​,C2​=876−4⋅22=788.
(57)
The new potentials are u=(0,5,−3) and v=(5,5,1). Enter (2,1), of reduced cost −7, on cycle +(2,1),−(1,1),+(1,3),−(2,3). The amount is min(14,56)=14. Thus
X∗​=​0140​02840​36420​​,C∗​=788−7⋅14=690.​
(58)
To certify optimality in the original transportation problem, take u=(0,5,−3) and v=(−2,5,1). Their entire reduced-cost matrix is
(cij​−ui​−vj​)=​7012​400​007​​≥0.
(59)
They satisfy dual feasibility, and their value is 5⋅84−3⋅40−2⋅14+5⋅68+78=690, equal to the shipment cost. The minimum transportation cost is therefore 690, with no unproved optimality assertion from the iterations alone.

Repeated differentiation of the Gaussian function gives Dne−x2=Pn​(x)e−x2, where P0​=1 and Pn+1​=Pn′​−2xPn​. Induction shows Pn​ has degree of a polynomial n and leading coefficient (−2)n: the differentiated term has lower degree, while multiplication by −2x raises it by one. Thus the Hermite polynomial Hn​=(−1)nPn​ has degree n and leading coefficient 2n.
For m<n, apply integration by parts n times to the Rodrigues expression:
∫−∞∞​Hn​Hm​e−x2dx=(−1)n∫−∞∞​Hm​Dne−x2dx=∫−∞∞​Hm(n)​e−x2dx=0.
(60)
All boundary terms vanish because each derivative of e−x2 is a polynomial times that exponential, and such products tend to zero at either infinity. The same result for m>n follows by symmetry of the inner product. The diagonal value is positive; indeed Hn(n)​=2nn! gives
(Hn​,Hm​)=2nn!π​δnm​.​
(61)
This proves the requested orthogonality as well as its normalization.

Use the Leibniz definition of the determinant:
detA=∑π∈Sn​​sgn(π)∏i=1n​ai,π(i)​.
(65)
For the permuted-column matrix, aijσ​=ai,σ(j)​. Reindex the sum by τ=σ∘π. The sign of a permutation is multiplicative, so sgn(π)=sgn(σ)sgn(τ). It follows directly that
det(Aσ)=sgn(σ)detA.
(66)
For the matrix transpose, the products in its determinant are ∏i​aπ(i),i​. Set j=π(i) to obtain ∏j​aj,π−1(j)​, and use sgn(π−1)=sgn(π). This proves det(At)=detA. These facts also show that equal columns, or equal rows by transposition, force the determinant to be zero: exchanging the equal pair leaves the matrix unchanged but changes the determinant's sign.
Let Mij​ be the matrix obtained by deleting row i and column j, with the empty determinant taken as one for n=1. Define the cofactor Cij​=(−1)i+jdetMij​ and the adjugate matrix by adj(A)ij​=Cji​. Grouping the Leibniz sum according to the column chosen in row i gives the cofactor expansion detA=∑k​aik​Cik​: deleting that row and its chosen column leaves a permutation of n−1 entries, with sign factor (−1)i+k. Therefore
(AadjA)ij​=∑k​aik​Cjk​.
(67)
When i=j this is detA. When i=j it is the cofactor expansion along row j of the matrix formed by replacing that row with row i; its remaining minors are unchanged, and its two equal rows give determinant zero. The column version proves the other product in the same way. Thus the adjugate identity is
Aadj(A)=adj(A)A=(detA)I,A−1=detAadj(A)​(detA=0).​
(68)
For the real matrices C,D, let p(t)=det(C+tD). The determinant definition makes this a real polynomial of degree of a polynomial at most n. Since C+iD is invertible, the allowed converse implies p(i)=0, so p is not the zero polynomial. It has at most n real roots of a polynomial. Choose a real λ outside those roots; the adjugate argument proves that C+λD is invertible.
Finally write the given complex similarity transformation as P=C+iD. The relation AP=PB, with A,B real, yields AC=CB and AD=DB by comparing real and imaginary parts. Choose the preceding λ and put Q=C+λD. Then AQ=QB, so
Q−1AQ=Bwith Q real and invertible.​
(69)
This proves real similarity from complex similarity by constructing a real intertwiner, rather than requiring C or D separately to be invertible.

The finite-dimensional inner product space has the orthogonal decomposition U=W⊕W⊥. Define τ(w+z)=w for w∈W, z∈W⊥. This is a linear map with image W, satisfies τ2=τ, and is self-adjoint by taking inner products between decomposed vectors. Hence it is an orthogonal projection.
Any other orthogonal projection with image W has kernel W⊥ by part (a); it is identity on W by idempotence and zero on its kernel. Its values are therefore forced to agree with τ, proving uniqueness.
If τ2​τ1​=0, every w1​∈W1​ has w1​=τ1​w1​, so τ2​w1​=0 and w1​∈W2⊥​. Conversely, if W1​⊂W2⊥​, every image τ1​u is killed by τ2​. Therefore

The time-independent Schrödinger equation is [−ℏ2∇2/(2m)+V]ψ=Eψ, with attractive Coulomb potential V(r)=−κ/r, where κ=e2/(4πε0​). Separating ψ=R(r)Yℓm​(θ,φ) uses the spherical harmonic angular eigenvalue −ℓ(ℓ+1) of the unit-sphere Laplacian. The radial kinetic contribution is −ℏ2(R′′+2R′/r)/(2m), the angular kinetic contribution is the centrifugal term ℏ2ℓ(ℓ+1)R/(2mr2), and the remaining term is the attractive potential energy. The right side is the energy eigenvalue times the radial wavefunction. Here the stated m neglects nuclear recoil; including it replaces the electron mass by the reduced mass.
For ℓ=0, substitution of the ground-state exponential gives
−2mℏ2​(α2−2α/r)−rκ​=E1​.
(84)
Its 1/r coefficient must vanish and its constant coefficient determines the energy, so
α=ℏ2mκ​=a0​1​,E1​=−2ℏ2mκ2​.​
(85)
Here a0​=ℏ2/(mκ) is the Bohr radius.
For R2​=N2​(r+b)e−βr, direct differentiation yields
R2′′​+r2​R2′​=N2​e−βr[β2(r+b)−4β+r2−2βb​].
(86)
Cancel the nonzero exponential in the radial Schrödinger equation and compare coefficients of r, the constant term, and 1/r. They give, respectively,
E2​=−2mℏ2β2​,m2ℏ2β​=κ,mℏ2​(βb−1)−κb=0.
(87)
Consequently
β=2a0​1​,b=−2a0​,E2​=−8ℏ2mκ2​=41​E1​.​
(88)
The positive decay constants ensure normalizability; the second radial wavefunction has one positive-radius node at 2a0​, as appropriate to the first radial excitation.
If the entire energy gap is carried by one photon, neglecting atomic recoil, conservation of energy gives the requested frequency
νgap​=hE2​−E1​​=8hℏ23mκ2​=8hℏ2(4πε0​)23me4​.​
(89)
There is a physical qualification: these are the 2s and 1s states, so the usual single-photon electric-dipole transition is forbidden by the electric-dipole selection rules for hydrogen. Explicitly, both angular factors are Y00​, and ∫∣Y00​∣2r^dΩ=0, so every component of ⟨1s∣r∣2s⟩ vanishes. The leading isolated-atom decay is instead two-photon emission, for which ν1​+ν2​=νgap​ and individual frequencies are not fixed. This metastability and the two-photon channel are documented in NIST's hydrogen spectral-data compilation. Thus the boxed answer is the energy-gap frequency under the printed single-photon assumption, rather than an assertion of an allowed electric-dipole line.
